opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think abductive reasoning is hard because it's the part of science that doesn't have a clean recipe. Deduction is about following rules from premises to conclusions, and AI is getting quite good at that, at least in formal settings like math proofs or code. Induction is about generalizing from lots of data, and that's essentially what modern machine learning does at scale. But abduction is different. It's inference to the best explanation. You see something surprising, an anomaly that doesn't fit, and you have to invent a hypothesis that would make it unsurprising.

The difficulty is that the space of possible explanations is basically unbounded. When Kepler looked at Tycho Brahe's data on Mars, the hard part wasn't fitting curves. He had to be willing to drop the circle, an assumption that had held for two thousand years, and consider an ellipse. That move requires knowing which of your background assumptions are load-bearing and which are just habits. Current models are very good at producing plausible-sounding hypotheses, but plausible usually means close to what's already in the training distribution. Real discovery often needs the hypothesis that looks implausible at first and turns out to be right.

There's also an evaluation problem. With deduction you can check the proof. With induction you can test on held-out data. With abduction, how do you score a new explanation before anyone has run the experiment? You need taste: a sense of simplicity, of explanatory power, of whether an idea opens new questions or just patches the old one. Scientists build that taste over years, through failed experiments and conversations with colleagues, and much of it is never written down. So it's thin in the data these systems learn from.

And finally, abduction in science is tied to action. A good scientist proposes an explanation and also designs the experiment that could kill it. That loop of hypothesize, test, get surprised, revise is slow, expensive, and grounded in the physical world. Until AI systems can close that loop, through automated labs or tight collaboration with experimentalists, they'll mostly be generating candidates rather than making discoveries. That's why I see it as the real frontier. It's where generating ideas meets the problem of knowing which ideas are worth believing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the reason abductive reasoning is so hard is that it's fundamentally different from the two modes of reasoning that current AI systems are actually good at.

Deduction is going from rules to conclusions. If you give a model the axioms and the inference steps, it can grind forward, and we've seen that it can do that quite well now, even on hard math problems. Induction is going from many examples to a pattern. That's basically what machine learning is. You show it a million images and it learns what a cat looks like. Both of these have a kind of closure to them. The answer is, in some sense, already contained in what you gave the system.

Abduction is the opposite direction. You see a surprising observation, something that doesn't fit, and you have to invent an explanation that would make it unsurprising. The explanation is not in the data. It's not derivable from the rules. You have to propose a new entity, a new mechanism, a new way of seeing the problem. Think about Darwin looking at finches, or someone looking at the anomalous precession of Mercury and saying, maybe the geometry of space itself is different. The leap is generative, and it's generative in a very specific way: the hypothesis has to be new, but it also has to be the right kind of new. Most new ideas are wrong.

And that's the second difficulty. The hypothesis space is essentially infinite. For any set of observations you can write down an unbounded number of explanations that fit. A good scientist doesn't search that space. They prune it almost instantly using taste, using a very deep physical or biological intuition about what kinds of explanations tend to be true in this world. That taste is learned over decades, it's largely tacit, and nobody has written it down because nobody can. So it's not in the training data in any explicit form.

The third thing I'd say is that abduction is inherently tied to being wrong a lot and getting feedback from the world. In my own experience doing experiments, most of what I thought was going on turned out to be something else. The reasoning only improves because you build something, it fails, and the failure teaches you. Language models today are mostly trained on the cleaned-up version of science, the paper where the story is told backwards from the result. They don't see the fifty dead ends. So they learn what a good explanation looks like after the fact, but not the process of arriving at one under genuine uncertainty.

So when people say AI will do scientific discovery, I'm optimistic, but I think we have to be honest about which part. Searching, deducing, pattern-matching, those are coming fast. The part where you look at something strange and say, I think the world works differently from how we assumed, and here is how, that's the frontier. And I don't think it gets solved by scale alone. It probably needs systems that can act in the world, get surprised, and update, in a loop that looks a lot more like a lab than like a library.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that abductive reasoning asks you to invent an explanation. With deduction, you have a theory and work out what should happen. With abduction, you observe something and ask, “What underlying mechanism could have produced this?” There can be many explanations consistent with the same observation.

In scientific discovery, you may also need to introduce a concept that isn’t already in your framework. If an experiment gives an unexpected result, is it measurement error, a missing variable, or evidence that your theory needs to change? The observation alone usually doesn’t tell you.

For AI, then, the challenge is more than generating a plausible hypothesis. It has to propose explanations that are testable, identify an experiment that distinguishes between them, and revise its explanation when the results disagree. That connection between imagining a mechanism and testing it against reality is what makes this such a difficult frontier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that scientific discovery often requires you to propose an explanation that isn’t already in the space you’re searching. Deduction starts with a theory and asks what follows. Induction looks at observations and tries to find a pattern. Abduction asks: What underlying mechanism could explain what I’m seeing?

And that’s a very underdetermined problem. Many different explanations can fit the same evidence. The challenge is to come up with a hypothesis that is plausible, but also testable—and then identify an experiment that distinguishes it from competing explanations.

For AI, that means more than generating a convincing scientific story. It has to recognize where existing explanations fail, propose something useful, and revise that proposal when experiments disagree. Connecting those steps into a reliable discovery process is what makes this such a difficult frontier.
